pr_body:
User defined functions are instance methods on the Script class.

Update lambdas and method references to capture the script `this`
reference.

Def method encoding string takes an extra char at index 1, whether
to capture the script reference.

For runtime fields, this means emit, which is an script instance
method already, now works in user defined functions.

Fixes: #69742
Refs: #68235
pr_title: Script: User funcs are script instance methods

review_comment: Do folk no longer need this?
It's private now, so inaccessible.  I'll bet I can provide a replacement getter that still provides useful information.

Could you explain what it's for? If no one's using it then I'd fine pitching it. If folks were using it they probably want to know. If it was just debugging stuff then cool, add whatever makes you feel good.
I updated it to use a getter.  It's just for debugging and development, for dumping the user tree.
What about throwing an exception here because it's not valid to ever set it accidentally? What you've got is fine now but it'd be kind to the next person working on it if we said "no".

There are lots of cases where we'll call this but the surrounding scope is not an LambdaScope, eg `byte get() {Byte.valueOf(5)} get()` in `FunctionTests.testReturnsAreUnboxedIfNeeded`.

In that case the scopes are `BlockScope` wrapped with a parent `FunctionScope`.
Cool. Could you leave a comment saying that it's ok that this is a noop? Just so I don't get confused when I look again in a few months.
Do you think it'd make the def handling code easier to read if you made a parsing ctor and used this object instead? It'd also let you assert the round trip and stuff.
It could have actual methods on it to build the signature of the factory method and stuff.
It's a decent amount of code but it does increase the likelihood of us finding a surprise early.  What do you think?

I talked with @stu-elastic on this one and he decided not to do it in this PR - it'd just be too big and we don't have enough coverage to make sure we don't accidentally break something. It's still a good change, but a follow up one.
